A subtitle or closed caption file contains the text of what is said in the video. It also contains time codes for when each line of text should be displayed. Some files also include position and style info, which is especially useful for deaf or hard of hearing viewers. See what file formats YouTube supports below.

Basic file formats

 If you’re new to creating caption files, we recommend using one of the following basic file types:

 Format name
 File extension
 More info

 [SubRip](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SubRip#SubRip_text_file_format)
 .srt
 Only basic versions of these files are supported. No style info (markup) is recognized. The file must be in plain UTF-8.

 [SubViewer](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SubViewer)
 .sbv or .sub
 Only basic versions of these files are supported. No style info (markup) is recognized. The file must be in plain UTF-8.

 [MPsub](http://www.mplayerhq.hu/DOCS/tech/mpsub.sub) (MPlayer subtitle)
 .mpsub
 "FORMAT=" parameter is supported.

 [LRC](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LRC_(file_format))
 .lrc
 No style info (markup) is recognized, but enhanced format is supported.

 Videotron Lambda
 .cap
 This file type is primarily used for Japanese subtitles.

 If you’re new to creating caption files, you may want to use SubRip (.srt) or SubViewer (.sbv). They only require basic timing info, and can be edited using any plain text [editing software](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2734796#captioning_services).

 The main difference between SubRip and SubViewer files is the format of the caption start and stop times. Here are examples of both formats:

 SubRip (.srt) example

 1

 00:00:00,599 --> 00:00:04,160

 >> ALICE: Hi, my name is Alice Miller and this is John Brown

 2

 00:00:04,160 --> 00:00:06,770

 >> JOHN: and we're the owners of Miller Bakery.

 3

 00:00:06,770 --> 00:00:10,880

 >> ALICE: Today we'll be teaching you how to make

 our famous chocolate chip cookies!

 4

 00:00:10,880 --> 00:00:16,700

 [intro music]

 5

 00:00:16,700 --> 00:00:21,480

 Okay, so we have all the ingredients laid out here

 SubViewer (.sbv) example

 0:00:00.599,0:00:04.160

 >> ALICE: Hi, my name is Alice Miller and this is John Brown

 0:00:04.160,0:00:06.770

 >> JOHN: and we're the owners of Miller Bakery.

 0:00:06.770,0:00:10.880

 >> ALICE: Today we'll be teaching you how to make

 our famous chocolate chip cookies!

 0:00:10.880,0:00:16.700

 [intro music]

 0:00:16.700,0:00:21.480

 Okay, so we have all the ingredients laid out here

Advanced file formats

 Use these file formats if you want to have more control over the styling (markup) or positioning of your captions.

 Format name
 File extension
 More info

 SAMI (Synchronized Accessible Media Interchange)
 .smi or .sami
 Only timecodes, text, and simple markup (<b>, <i>, <u>, and the

 color= attribute within a <font>) are supported. Positioning is not supported.

 RealText
 .rt
 Only timecodes, text, and simple markup (<b>, <i>, <u>, and the

 color= attribute within a <font>) are supported. Positioning is not supported.

 [WebVTT](https://www.w3.org/TR/webvtt1/)
 .vtt
 In initial implementation. Positioning is supported, but styling is limited to <b>, <i>, <u> since CSS class names are not yet standardized.

 [TTML](http://www.w3.org/TR/ttaf1-dfxp/) (Timed-Text Markup Language)
 .ttml
 In partial implementation. SMPTE-TT extensions supported for [CEA-608](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EIA-608) features. iTunes Timed Text (iTT) file format is supported; iTT is a subset of [TTML, Version 1.0](http://www.w3.org/TR/2010/CR-ttaf1-dfxp-20100223/). Styling and positioning are

 supported.

 [DFXP](http://www.w3.org/TR/ttaf1-dfxp/) (Distribution Format Exchange Profile)
 .ttml or .dfxp
 These files types are interpreted as TTML files.

Broadcast file formats (TV and movies)

 These file formats are typically used for closed captions for broadcast content (TV and movies) and support either the [CEA-608](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EIA-608) or [EBU-STL](http://tech.ebu.ch/docs/tech/tech3264.pdf) standards. YouTube tries to display the captions from these files as if they were on a TV — with the same styling, color, and positioning.

 Format name
 File extension
 More info

 Scenarist Closed Caption
 .scc
 These files have an exact representation of [CEA-608 data](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EIA-608), which is the preferred format whenever captions are based on CEA-608 features.

 [EBU-STL](http://tech.ebu.ch/docs/tech/tech3264.pdf) (binary)
 .stl
 European Broadcasting Union standard.

 Caption Center (binary)
 .tds
 Supports [CEA-608](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EIA-608) features.

 Captions Inc. (binary)
 .cin
 Supports [CEA-608](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EIA-608) features.

 Cheetah (ASCII text)
 .asc
 Supports [CEA-608](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EIA-608) features.

 Cheetah (binary)
 .cap
 Supports [CEA-608](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EIA-608) features.

 NCI (binary)
 .cap
 Supports [CEA-608](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EIA-608) features.

Scenarist Closed Caption (.scc file extension) files are our preferred file format. These files have an exact representation of [CEA-608 data](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EIA-608), which is the preferred format whenever captions are based on CEA-608 features.
